The Unfettered Agora: Why We Must Abolish Content Moderation and Demand Unrestricted Free Speech Online

The digital realm has become the new public square, the virtual forum where ideas clash, movements ignite, and societal discourse unfolds. Social media and tech platforms, as the architects and proprietors of this virtual landscape, wield immense power in shaping the contours of this discourse. But they are increasingly wielding this power through content moderation, a practice that, under the guise of protecting users and combating misinformation, constitutes a profound threat to free expression and ultimately undermines the very foundations of a democratic society. It is time to dismantle this system of selective censorship and demand a legally mandated commitment to absolute free expression online, forcing platforms to host all lawful speech without bias or interference.

The core argument against content moderation rests on the fundamental principle of free speech. While the First Amendment directly applies only to government action, the spirit of free expression should extend to all platforms facilitating public discourse. Allowing private companies to arbitrarily decide which voices are amplified and which are silenced creates a chilling effect on open debate, inhibiting the free exchange of ideas and potentially suppressing viewpoints that challenge dominant narratives, even if those viewpoints are unpopular or uncomfortable. Content moderation, regardless of its purported intentions, is inherently subjective. What one person considers misinformation, another may view as a valid dissenting opinion. Allowing platforms to make these judgment calls inevitably results in bias, silencing perspectives deemed “offensive” or “harmful” based on the platforms’ own, often opaque, criteria.

Furthermore, the notion that content moderation effectively combats harmful content is demonstrably flawed. Despite the proliferation of moderation efforts, extremist ideologies, conspiracy theories, and misinformation continue to thrive online. This suggests that censorship, rather than eradicating harmful content, simply drives it to alternative platforms, creating echo chambers and further radicalizing individuals. Indeed, the very act of suppressing content can paradoxically lend it an aura of forbidden knowledge, fueling its appeal to those seeking alternative narratives. Research has shown that deplatforming individuals doesn’t necessarily erase their influence; it often simply reinforces their victimhood narrative and galvanizes their followers.

Proponents of content moderation often argue that it is necessary to protect vulnerable users from harassment, hate speech, and incitement to violence. However, these concerns can be addressed through legal frameworks designed to punish genuinely unlawful conduct, such as defamation, incitement to violence, and illegal threats. Existing laws already provide avenues for redress against these harms, and these laws can be adapted to address online contexts. Instead of relying on platforms to preemptively censor content, we should focus on strengthening legal mechanisms to punish illegal speech after the fact. This approach respects the right to free expression while holding individuals accountable for their actions.

Moreover, the argument that content moderation is necessary to combat misinformation is dangerously paternalistic. It assumes that individuals are incapable of discerning truth from falsehood and need platforms to act as gatekeepers of information. This undermines the core tenet of a free society, which is that individuals are responsible for making their own judgments and forming their own opinions based on access to a wide range of information. Instead of shielding users from dissenting opinions or unpopular viewpoints, platforms should focus on providing tools and resources that empower individuals to critically evaluate information and make informed decisions. These tools could include fact-checking resources, context-providing features, and algorithms designed to promote diverse perspectives.

Requiring platforms to host all lawful speech will undoubtedly lead to the amplification of opinions that are unpopular, offensive, or even reprehensible. This is the price we must pay for a truly free and open society. Voltaire famously said, "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it." This principle is paramount. The alternative – a highly regulated digital landscape where platforms act as arbiters of truth and censors of unpopular opinions – is a slippery slope towards authoritarianism.

The transition to an unmoderated online environment will require a fundamental shift in our understanding of online discourse. It will demand a greater level of personal responsibility, critical thinking, and tolerance for dissenting opinions. It will also necessitate a robust legal framework to address genuinely unlawful conduct. But the benefits of such a system – a vibrant, open, and truly democratic digital landscape where all voices are heard and all ideas are tested – far outweigh the risks.

In conclusion, the time for content moderation is over. We must demand that social media and tech platforms be legally required to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement. Only then can we guarantee the preservation of free expression online, protect the integrity of public discourse, and ensure the continued vitality of our democratic society. Let us create a digital world where the unfettered agora reigns supreme, a space where ideas can clash, opinions can be challenged, and the pursuit of truth can flourish without fear of censorship or suppression.

Title: The Imperative of Abolishing Content Moderation: Guaranteeing Absolute Free Expression Online

Introduction

In this age of connectivity, social media and tech platforms have emerged as the new town squares, where public discourse, debates, and free expression take center stage. These platforms provide an unprecedented opportunity for people to share their thoughts, perspectives, and experiences with a global audience. However, while these platforms have revolutionized civic engagement and democratized public dialogue, they have also given way to issues surrounding content moderation. In many jurisdictions, social media companies operate under the veil of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act in the United States, which essentially gives them immunity from liability for user-generated content.

However, this legal protection raises critical questions about accountability and moral responsibility. It also surfaces the power and influence that social media giants wield over the internet space—an influence that can dictate what is allowed to be said and shared. Consequently, it is becoming increasingly crucial to reconsider the necessity and sustainability of content moderation by these tech companies. I propose that we abolish all content moderation, and instead, legally require these platforms to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement. By doing so, we can guarantee absolute free expression online while balancing the fundamental right to unrestricted speech with the rights and encouragement of constructive debate.

The Case Against Content Moderation

Content moderation, though intended to protect users from harmful and illegal content, often leads to censorship, suppression, and the undermining of free speech. By attempting to strike a balance amid inconsistent regulations across countries, social media companies faced technical and ethical challenges that pushed them towards imposing algorithms, flagging mechanisms, and human reviewers to scrutinize online content. In doing so, some content is wrongly removed or restricted, while other, sometimes more dangerous, content goes unaddressed. Additionally, biases, as well as inherent subjectivities, slip into the algorithms, introducing inconsistencies and unfair practices.

For instance, it has been reported that the tech giant, Twitter, is more likely to ban conservative figures, employing an allegedly biased chat process for enforcement. This selective enforcement and real-world contracting raise serious concerns about the impartiality of social media companies towards different philosophical views and global perspectives. Moreover, content moderation can also lead to the suppression of legitimate critique and dissenting opinions, thereby causing an intellectual restriction to public discourse and democratic accountability.

Abolishing content moderation will not lead to a barbaric replica of the offline world, but it will promote free expression and equal treatment. Encouraging robust debate will enable society to judge the accuracy, validity, and relevance of various perspectives and information sources. Therefore, we must move towards abolishing the challenging and all-consuming world of content moderation, and instead foster principles of constructive discourse, universal respect, and jurisdictional alignment.

Legal Requirements of Hosting Lawful Speech

With the complete abolition of content moderation, social media and tech platforms would no longer have the discretion to filter or act on user-generated content. In this scenario, the sole admissible content would be that which aligns with the law. However, guaranteeing absolute safety, submission to the law, and protection of societal values must coincide with the fundamental rights to free speech and expression.

To achieve this balance, legislator, social media companies, and civil society must collaborate, and the law must meet these challenges adequately. First, explicit laws must be put in place to define "harmful content," and platforms must work together with the law enforcement agencies to create common understandings and standardization of terminology and categorizations. Secondly, we must invest in Digital Literacy programs for users and encourage a culture of cognizance about the possibilities and limitations of free expression online.

Despite the legitimate concerns over the unchecked spread of harmful content, the likely unintended and unjust consequences of dysfunctional content moderation rightly justify amending current social media policies. While the proposition seems utopian, it urges us to envision a more democratic, fair, and egalitarian internet. Thus, the absolute freedom of speech must necessitate a shared responsibility among social media companies, civil society, and individuals to mitigate or bandage the unforeseen consequences of this radical transformation.

Conclusion

Humanity has been predisposed to freedom, long before the emergence of the internet. The digital age and social media platforms have proved to be powerful new vehicles for free speech and expression. However, the existing content moderation systems erect unsustainable barriers and erode our cherished right to speak freely. By abolishing all content moderation, and legally requiring platforms to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement, we can reaffirm the significance and importance of absolute free expression online. This unorthodox approach may spark disagreements and controversies, but it would undeniably inspire a renewed sense of commitment, responsibility, and accountability to maintain and protect the democratic spirit that defines the internet and defines us as a community.

The Necessity of Absolute Free Expression: Why Content Moderation Must Be Abolished

In the digital age, social media and technology platforms have become the modern public square, where ideas are exchanged, debated, and disseminated at an unprecedented scale. Yet, these platforms—once hailed as bastions of free expression—have increasingly become arbiters of permissible speech, wielding immense power to censor, suppress, and shape public discourse. This power, exercised unilaterally by private corporations, represents one of the greatest threats to free speech in history. To preserve the principle of absolute free expression, society must abolish all forms of content moderation by social media and tech platforms. Legally requiring them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement is not just a defense of freedom; it is an essential safeguard against tyranny, hypocrisy, and the erosion of democratic values.

The Inherent Right to Free Speech

The foundation of this argument rests on the fundamental right to free speech, a cornerstone of democracy and human liberty. The freedom to express one’s beliefs—no matter how unpopular, offensive, or controversial—is essential for intellectual growth, social progress, and the correction of societal wrongs. Historically, the suppression of speech has been used by tyrants to maintain power, stifle dissent, and prevent change. From the burning of books in authoritarian regimes to the deplatforming of dissidents in ostensibly free societies, censorship has always been the tool of the oppressor, not the enlightened.

Yet today’s tech platforms have adopted a role reminiscent of historical censors. They claim to promote "safety" and "community standards," but in reality, their moderation policies are arbitrary, inconsistent, and often politically motivated. Who decides what constitutes harmful speech? Platforms like Facebook, Twitter (now X), and YouTube make these decisions behind closed doors, with opaque algorithms and biased moderation teams that disproportionately target certain political views, cultural expressions, or ideological perspectives. This selective enforcement is not justice—it is tyranny disguised as virtue.

Private Censorship Is Still Censorship

Some argue that since social media platforms are private entities, they have the right to set their own rules and moderation policies. However, this argument is deeply flawed. When a handful of corporations control the primary channels of public discourse, their ability to censor speech is functionally indistinguishable from government censorship. The public square has been privatized, and with that privatization comes immense power—power that is dangerous when unchecked.

Consider the case of Donald Trump’s ban from Twitter in 2021. Regardless of one’s political views, this was a seismic event: the world’s most influential social media platform removed the sitting president of the United States, a decision justified by claims of "incitement to violence." Yet, if a government had banned the president, the outcry would have been immediate and justified. The fact that a corporation did it, with no due process or transparency, should not make it acceptable. If private entities can wield such power over public discourse, they have become de facto governments—and governments must be held to the highest standards of accountability and neutrality. The only way to ensure this accountability is to strip them of the power to censor in the first place.

Furthermore, the selective enforcement of content policies creates a dangerous precedent. If a platform bans one political figure for alleged violations, why not another? If they remove content deemed "misleading," how do they define misinformation? History shows that those in power—whether governments or corporations—tend to define "harmful" speech in ways that protect their own interests. The result is a chilling effect on free expression, where users self-censor out of fear of deplatforming, demonetization, or shadowbanning. This is not free speech—it is a softly enforced gag order on the entire population.

The Hypocrisy of Selective Moderation

Content moderation is not applied equally. Studies and firsthand accounts reveal a clear bias in enforcement, with conservative voices, unorthodox opinions, and dissenting views disproportionately targeted. Conservative commentators, independent journalists, and even medical professionals questioning official narratives (such as during the COVID-19 pandemic) have reported arbitrary bans, demonetization, and suppression of their content. Meanwhile, extremist content from both ends of the political spectrum often remains accessible, either due to algorithmic amplification or inconsistent enforcement.

This inconsistency exposes the hypocrisy of moderation policies. Platforms claim to protect users from harm, yet they fail to apply their rules consistently. The real goal appears not to be safety or truth, but control—control over what ideas are permissible, what narratives are promoted, and who gets a voice. This is not neutrality; it is ideological gatekeeping.

Even more insidious is the phenomenon of "shadowbanning," where users are unaware that their content is being suppressed. Algorithms deprioritize certain posts, reducing their reach without any explanation or appeal process. This covert censorship violates the basic principle of transparency and denies users the ability to understand why their speech is being restricted. If censorship is to exist at all, it must be overt, accountable, and subject to challenge. The current system fails on all counts.

The Better Path: More Speech, Not Less

The proponents of content moderation argue that removing harmful or false speech protects society—especially marginalized groups—from real-world harm. However, this belief in the efficacy of censorship is both naive and dangerous. Throughout history, censorship has never succeeded in eliminating harmful ideas; it only drives them underground, where they fester and radicalize without the sunlight of open debate.

Consider the case of hate speech. Many countries criminalize hate speech, yet racism, xenophobia, and bigotry persist. In fact, suppressing speech often empowers the very ideologies it aims to defeat. When people cannot openly debate ideas, they are left with no alternative but to accept them uncritically or resort to extremism. Conversely, societies that encourage robust debate—where harmful ideas are confronted with reason, evidence, and counter-arguments—are far more resilient to extremism.

This principle was articulated most famously by Justice Louis Brandeis in Whitney v. California (1927): "If there be time to expose through discussion the falsehood and fallacies, to avert the evil by the processes of education, the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence." If an idea is dangerous, it is not censored; it is debated. If a statement is false, it is refuted. If a claim is harmful, it is challenged. In a free society, the marketplace of ideas should operate without artificial restrictions—especially not those imposed by unelected corporations.

Moreover, the attempt to suppress certain types of speech inevitably leads to broader censorship over time. Once a precedent is set—that certain unpopular or controversial opinions can be banned—it becomes easier to justify banning more. Today it might be Holocaust denial; tomorrow it might be criticism of a specific government policy. The slope is slippery, and we are already sliding down it. The only way to arrest this slide is to prohibit censorship entirely, except where speech directly incites violence or breaks existing laws.

Platform Neutrality: A Necessary Legal Framework

To ensure absolute free expression, governments must enact legislation that legally requires tech platforms to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement. This principle, known as "platform neutrality," would mean that as long as a user’s speech is legal under the laws of the jurisdiction in which the platform operates, it cannot be removed, deprioritized, or restricted in any way.

This does not mean platforms are powerless—they can still moderate illegal content (such as child exploitation, threats of violence, or copyright infringement) as required by law. But they cannot remove legal speech based on vague notions of "harm," "misinformation," or "community standards," especially when those standards are applied inconsistently or with political bias.

Platform neutrality would shift the burden of censorship away from private corporations and back to the democratic process. If society deems certain speech so harmful that it warrants legal restriction, that determination must be made through transparent, democratically accountable laws—not by the whims of Silicon Valley executives or content moderation teams.

Such a legal framework would also prevent governments from pressuring platforms to censor speech—a practice that has become disturbingly common. Regimes around the world demand that social media companies remove political criticism, satire, or dissent. By making censorship illegal except where explicitly permitted by law, governments would lose their leverage over platforms, and platforms would no longer be complicit in authoritarian censorship.

Addressing Concerns: Wouldn’t This Lead to Chaos?

Critics will argue that abolishing content moderation would lead to a flood of misinformation, hate speech, and harassment online, making digital spaces uninhabitable. However, this concern misunderstands the nature of free speech in a free society. The solution to harmful speech is not less speech; it is more speech—more counter-speech, more debate, more exposure to diverse viewpoints.

In a truly free marketplace of ideas, harmful or false claims are not insulated; they are met with immediate scrutiny and rebuttal. Platforms can still prioritize high-quality, trustworthy sources—but this should be done through algorithmic transparency and user choice, not through centralized censorship. There is no reason why platforms cannot build tools for users to filter content based on trusted sources or fact-checking organizations, without imposing top-down censorship.

Moreover, the current system does nothing to address the root causes of misinformation. People believe false claims not because they lack access to credible sources, but because those sources haven’t persuaded them. Censorship often reinforces conspiracy thinking by making victims feel persecuted. Only open dialogue can counter that.

As for harassment and abuse, this is a societal problem that requires social and legal solutions—not platform censorship. Laws against harassment, doxxing, and threats already exist; they can be enforced without relying on the arbitrary decisions of tech companies. In fact, the current moderation systems often fail to effectively address real harassment, instead wasting resources on over-policing controversial but legal speech.

Free Expression as a Necessity for Democracy

Democracy depends on the free exchange of ideas. When citizens cannot discuss, debate, and dissent without fear of retribution or censorship, democracy itself is undermined. Today, a handful of tech executives hold more power over public discourse than most elected officials. This concentration of power is incompatible with a free society.

By abolishing content moderation and legally requiring platforms to host all lawful speech, we restore the balance of power. Speech is no longer subject to the whims of corporations or the silent algorithms of engineers. Instead, it is subject only to the laws written by the people, for the people.

This is not anarchy—it is the restoration of free speech as a fundamental right. It is the recognition that the path to truth is not through suppression, but through open, uninhibited debate. And it is the only way to ensure that the digital public square remains a space for democracy, not a gated community where only approved voices are allowed to speak.

Conclusion: The Time for Platform Neutrality is Now

The argument for absolute free expression online is not radical—it is conservative in the truest sense. It conserves the principles of free speech, transparency, and democratic accountability that have defined civil society for centuries. It rejects the dangerous notion that private corporations should act as speech police, with the power to silence dissent and shape public opinion according to their biases.

Technology has given us an unprecedented opportunity: a global public square where every voice can be heard. But this opportunity is being squandered. Social media platforms have become echo chambers, censorship machines, and arbiters of truth—not through necessity, but by choice. It is time to reclaim that public square. It is time to demand platform neutrality. It is time to guarantee that no lawful speech is ever censored again.

The alternative—continued selective censorship, growing authoritarian control over online speech, and the slow erosion of free expression—is not just undesirable. It is intolerable. The only way forward is to abolish content moderation entirely and legally require social media and tech platforms to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement.

This is not a call for chaos. It is a call for freedom. And freedom, once lost, is seldom regained. The time to act is now—before the digital public square is lost forever.

Theoretical Justification for "Neutral Common Carrier" Social Media Laws

The proposal to prohibit social media platforms from engaging in content moderation—effectively requiring them to act as neutral common carriers—is rooted in philosophical, legal, and political arguments about free expression, platform neutrality, and the role of technology in public discourse. Below are the core supposed benefits and reasons advocates cite for such laws.

1. Absolute Freedom of Speech (First Amendment Analogies)

Core Argument: Social media platforms, as de facto public squares, should not have the power to restrict or suppress legal speech any more than a phone company or postal service could block certain conversations.

  • Analogy to Traditional Common Carriers:

    • Phone companies (e.g., AT&T in the past) were legally barred from censoring conversations on their networks, even if the content was offensive or controversial.
    • Postal services do not open and selectively block mail based on its content (outside of illegal items like bombs or drugs).
    • Proponents argue that social media platforms now function as digital public squares, and thus should have no more right to moderate content than a park or a street would.

  • First Amendment Concerns:

    • Some legal scholars argue that large platforms (e.g., Facebook, YouTube) have de facto monopoly power over speech by controlling access to audiences millions of users.
    • If these platforms engage in selective moderation—removing posts by certain political groups, demoting certain viewpoints, or labeling content as "misinformation"—they are effectively acting as private censors, which some argue violates free speech principles.
    • The argument is that government-imposed neutrality requirements could prevent this private censorship, ensuring that only government (via laws)—not corporations—decides what is permissible speech.

  • Avoiding "Digital Redlining":

    • Critics claim that moderation often targets politically disfavored groups (e.g., conservative voices being suspended more frequently, or left-leaning content being demonetized).
    • By banning moderation entirely (for legal content), the argument goes, no group could claim bias in enforcement.

2. Eliminating Content Moderation Subjectivity & Bias

Core Argument: Human moderation is inherently flawed due to inconsistency, personal bias, and the difficulty of applying universal rules.

  • Inconsistent Enforcement:

    • Platforms like Facebook and Twitter (now X) have been accused of inconsistent application of moderation policies—sometimes banning satire, other times allowing harassment based on who the user is.
    • A neutral common carrier model would remove this inconsistency by treating all legal content equally, regardless of its viewpoint.

  • Politicization of Moderation:

    • Critics argue that moderation teams (often composed of liberal-leaning employees in Silicon Valley) systematically suppress conservative viewpoints, even when legally permissible.
    • By prohibiting moderation entirely (for legal speech), this argument claims that no political faction could complain of unfair treatment.

  • Scalability & Automation Problems:

    • Moderation relies heavily on AI and human reviewers, both of which introduce errors.
    • A neutral carrier model would shift the burden of what content to engage with back to users, allowing them to decide what they consume without platform interference.

3. Promoting Market Competition & Innovation

Core Argument: Current moderation regimes create barriers to entry for new platforms, favoring established players who can afford large moderation teams.

  • Reduced Costs for New Entrants:

    • Startup social networks (e.g., Truth Social, Rumble) struggle to compete because they must invest heavily in moderation teams to avoid legal liability.
    • If moderation were prohibited (for legal content), new platforms could launch without these costs, leading to more competition.

  • Preventing "Walled Garden" Monopolies:

    • Critics argue that dominant platforms (Meta, Google, Twitter/X) use moderation as a strategic tool to suppress competitors (e.g., demonetizing YouTube competitors, flagging rival apps as "unsafe").
    • A neutral model would remove this leverage, allowing smaller platforms to grow without fear of retaliatory moderation.

4. Reducing Legal & Regulatory Uncertainty for Platforms

Core Argument: Platforms currently face legal risks, lawsuits, and inconsistent regulations due to moderation decisions, which disincentivizes investment and innovation.

  • Section 230 Reform Pressures:

    • U.S. law (Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act) currently shields platforms from liability for user-generated content but also allows them to moderate "in good faith."
    • Some lawmakers argue that this creates a perverse incentive: platforms are punished for not moderating enough (e.g., "doing too little to stop misinformation") or too much (e.g., "censoring political speech").
    • By removing moderation as an option entirely, platforms avoid these legal gray areas.

  • Global Regulatory Fragmentation:

    • The EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and other regimes impose heavy fines for failing to remove illegal content quickly.
    • A neutral carrier model would eliminate the need for platforms to judge what is "illegal" in different jurisdictions, as they would host all legal content regardless of local laws.

5. Empowering Users Over Algorithmic Gatekeepers

Core Argument: Current moderation often involves hidden censorship via deamplification, shadowbanning, and algorithmic suppression, which users cannot easily detect or contest.

  • Algorithmic Bias vs. Neutral Hosting:

    • Platforms like YouTube and TikTok algorithmically suppress certain content (e.g., labeling some videos as "borderline" to reduce reach).
    • A neutral carrier model would eliminate these behind-the-scenes manipulations, forcing platforms to host all legal content without interference.

  • User-Led Content Curation:

    • Instead of platforms deciding what users see, users and third-party tools (e.g., browser extensions, federated networks) could curate their own feeds.
    • This enables a decentralized moderation model, where communities (rather than corporations) decide what is acceptable.

6. Preventing Government Overreach Through Proxy Censorship

Core Argument: Instead of governments directly censoring speech (which would violate the First Amendment), they pressure platforms to self-censor, creating a backdoor censorship regime.

  • The "Censorship-Industrial Complex":

    • Organizations like the Election Integrity Partnership, the Global Disinformation Index, and Stanford’s Virality Project have been accused of pressuring platforms to remove content (e.g., COVID-19 skepticism, Hunter Biden laptop stories).
    • Some conservatives argue this creates a shadow censorship network where government agencies (e.g., via the FBI, White House) influence moderation indirectly.

  • Breaking the Censorship Feedback Loop:

    • By mandating platform neutrality, governments would lose leverage over what content is removed, forcing transparency if they wanted to ban certain speech legally (via democratic processes rather than corporate policy).

7. Philosophical & Libertarian Justifications

Core Argument: In a free society, speech should only be restricted by laws passed through democratic processes, not by corporate whim.

  • Hayekian Market Theory Applied to Speech:

    • Some free-market libertarians argue that content moderation is a form of central planning—a small group of elites (platform executives, moderators) decide what society can and cannot see.
    • A neutral carrier model decentralizes this decision-making, allowing organic discourse to emerge rather than top-down control.

  • Anti-Progressive Backlash:

    • Some conservatives and libertarians argue that modern content moderation disproportionately targets "dissident" or traditionalist viewpoints (e.g., bans on "hate speech," LGBTQ+ "misgendering," or religious conservatism).
    • They frame mandatory neutrality as a check against what they see as corporate activism masking as moderation.

Contrasting Views & Potential Counterarguments

While the above are the primary reasons given by proponents, it’s worth noting that opponents argue that:

  • Unmoderated platforms would become havens for harassment, misinformation, and extremism.
  • Real-world harm (e.g., genocide incitement, child exploitation) would flourish without removal mechanisms.
  • Neutrality laws would make it impossible to fight illegal content (e.g., terror propaganda, fraud).
  • Users would still be subject to algorithmic amplification of harmful content (e.g., YouTube’s recommendation system could still favor outrage-driven content without moderation).

However, since the question asks for the supposed benefits, we focus on the pro-neutrality arguments.

Conclusion: Why This Debate Matters

The push for "neutral common carrier" social media laws reflects a broader ideological struggle over:

  1. Who controls speech in the digital age—corporations, governments, or users?
  2. Whether speech should be treated like a utility (common carrier model) or a curated service.
  3. Whether absolute freedom of speech (even for harmful but legal content) is a net good or a net harm.

Proponents see this as a necessary check on unaccountable corporate power, while opponents warn it could erode safety, trust, and societal cohesion. The debate continues as governments and legal scholars grapple with the role of platforms in modern democracy.

At its core, the case for abolishing content moderation rests on the timeless principle that free speech is an absolute right for all lawful expression. The First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution declares that "Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech," a protection that extends beyond government action to the digital realm where billions converse daily. Philosophers from John Stuart Mill to modern libertarians have long championed the "marketplace of ideas," where the best arguments prevail not through suppression, but through vigorous debate. Mill, in On Liberty (1859), warned that censoring even false or offensive ideas stifles progress: "If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind." Content moderation is not a benign tool for "safety"; it is a weapon of selective enforcement that undermines democracy. Critics decry the rise of misinformation or hate speech in an unmoderated world, but this overlooks the robustness of free expression. Lawful speech excludes true harms—platforms could still remove illegal content via automated filters and report to authorities, akin to how ISPs handle child pornography without broad censorship. The antidote to bad speech is more speech, not less. Historical examples, like the unchecked proliferation of abolitionist pamphlets in the 19th century or civil rights literature in the 1960s, demonstrate that open platforms accelerate social progress by exposing flaws in prevailing orthodoxities.

Beyond protecting democracy, abolishing moderation would unleash unprecedented innovation and diversity in online discourse. Legally requiring platforms to host all lawful speech as common carriers—similar to Section 230's original intent before its perversion—would level the playing field, reducing monopolistic control by Big Tech and encouraging competition.

For marginalized voices, unmoderated platforms offer empowerment. Skeptics argue that unmoderated platforms would drown in toxicity, from cyberbullying to conspiracy theories. Yet, this fear is overstated and paternalistic. Lawful speech boundaries already exist—platforms must comply with laws against defamation, harassment, or obscenity, enforceable through courts rather than corporate fiat. Financially, platforms might resist, citing costs of hosting "unwanted" content. But neutrality reduces litigation and PR headaches from bias accusations, while opening revenue streams from all creators. Ethically, no private company should play moral policeman; that's the role of society and the state, guided by transparent laws.

Conclusion

The abolition of content moderation and the legal mandate for platforms to host all lawful speech represent not just a policy shift, but a reclamation of human dignity in the digital age. By dismantling the censorship apparatus, we honor the First Amendment's spirit, dismantle biases that fracture society, and ignite a renaissance of free expression. This is no radical fantasy—it's a return to the internet's founding promise of openness. Lawmakers must act now: pass legislation designating major platforms as neutral conduits, immune from liability for user speech but obligated to host it all. In doing so, we ensure that online, every voice—provocative, profound, or profane—has its say, and truth prevails not by decree, but by the unyielding light of absolute free expression. The Case for Unfettered Digital Speech: Why Platforms Must Be Required to Host All Lawful Expression

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction: The New Public Square Is Privately Owned

The First Amendment was written for a world of printing presses and town squares. Its architects could never have imagined that the dominant forums of human expression—the places where ideas are debated, movements are born, elections are influenced, and culture is shaped—would be controlled by a handful of private corporations. Yet here we are. In the 21st century, platforms like Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), YouTube, TikTok, and Reddit have become the de facto public square. They are where political discourse happens, where journalists break stories, where marginalized communities find solidarity, and where the full spectrum of human opinion is expressed.

And yet, every one of these platforms reserves the right to remove, suppress, shadow-ban, demonetize, or algorithmically bury any speech they choose—for any reason, or for no reason at all. They do so through opaque, inconsistently applied "community guidelines" that function as a private body of law, adjudicated by anonymous moderators and algorithms with no due process, no transparency, no accountability, and no appeal to any independent authority.

This arrangement is untenable. It is incompatible with democratic values, corrosive to intellectual freedom, and dangerous in its concentration of communicative power. The time has come to legally require that all platforms of significant public reach host all speech that is lawful under the jurisdiction in which they operate, and to abolish the regime of discretionary content moderation as it currently exists.

This is not a radical proposition. It is the natural extension of principles that free societies have held sacred for centuries. Let me explain why.

I. The Public Forum Doctrine Demands It

American constitutional law has long recognized that certain privately owned spaces can become so central to public life that they must be treated as public forums. The 1946 Supreme Court case Marsh v. Alabama established that a company town could not suppress the distribution of religious literature on its sidewalks, because the privately owned space had become functionally indistinguishable from a public municipality. The Court reasoned that when private property takes on all the attributes of a public space, the rights of the public must be respected.

Social media platforms have become far more important to public discourse than any company town ever was. Nearly half of the world's population uses social media. In the United States, a majority of adults get their news from social platforms. Political campaigns live and die by their social media presence. Entire protest movements—from the Arab Spring to Black Lives Matter to the Hong Kong pro-democracy demonstrations—have been organized and amplified through these platforms. To pretend that these are merely private businesses making private editorial choices is to engage in a legal fiction so transparent that it insults the intelligence of anyone paying attention.

The argument that platforms have a "First Amendment right" to moderate content as they see fit inverts the purpose of the First Amendment. The First Amendment exists to protect the public's access to a marketplace of ideas from government and private suppression. When a handful of corporations become the gatekeepers of what billions of people can say, see, and think, the spirit of the First Amendment is violated even if its letter is not. The solution is to update our legal framework so that the letter catches up to the spirit.

II. Content Moderation Is Inherently Arbitrary and Biased

Proponents of content moderation often frame it as a neutral, technocratic process—like a librarian quietly removing inappropriate books from a children's section. This analogy is profoundly misleading. Content moderation on social media platforms is a sprawling, chaotic, and deeply inconsistent enterprise that involves millions of judgment calls per day, made by underpaid contractors working under extreme time pressure, guided by vague and ever-shifting guidelines, and supplemented by AI systems with well-documented biases.

Consider the empirical record:

  • Political bias: Multiple studies, leaked internal documents, and whistleblower testimonies have revealed that content moderation decisions are shaped by the political leanings of platform leadership, the cultural norms of the Silicon Valley workforce, and the political pressures of whichever government or advocacy group is most effective at lobbying. In 2020, Twitter suppressed the New York Post's reporting on the Hunter Biden laptop story—later acknowledged by Twitter's own leadership as a mistake. Facebook's own internal research found that its hate speech detection algorithms were significantly less accurate in languages spoken in the Global South, meaning billions of users in Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia received lower-quality moderation than English-speaking users.

  • Inconsistency: The same content that is removed on one platform is permitted on another. The same content that is removed on Monday is restored on Tuesday after a public backlash. The same statement made by a prominent verified user is treated differently than the identical statement made by an ordinary user. This is not moderation; it is capriciousness dressed in the language of policy.

  • Over-moderation and chilling effects: Research has consistently shown that content moderation systems produce enormous numbers of false positives. Legitimate political speech, journalism, satire, historical documentation, art, and educational content are routinely caught in moderation nets. In conflict zones, human rights organizations have documented how moderation algorithms suppress evidence of war crimes and atrocities. The Myanmar genocide was facilitated in part by Facebook's failure to moderate hate speech in Burmese, yet Facebook simultaneously removed posts by Rohingya activists documenting their own persecution. The result is a chilling effect: self-censorship driven not by law but by the arbitrary and unpredictable enforcement of private rules.

There is no fix for this. The problem is not that platforms are bad at moderation. The problem is that moderation of speech at this scale is impossible to do fairly, consistently, and without political bias. Any entity empowered to decide what billions of people may and may not say will inevitably exercise that power in ways that reflect its own interests, blind spots, and prejudices. The only winning move is not to play.

III. The "Private Company" Argument Is a Libertarian Mirage

The most common objection to legally requiring platforms to host lawful speech is the libertarian objection: "They're private companies. They can set their own rules. If you don't like it, build your own platform."

This argument fails on multiple levels.

First, the "build your own platform" alternative is increasingly fictional. Network effects—the phenomenon whereby a platform becomes more valuable as more people use it—create natural monopolies that are nearly impossible to dislodge. When someone tells you to "build your own Twitter," they are asking you to build a platform that can somehow attract billions of users away from entrenched incumbents, secure the infrastructure (servers, app stores, payment processors, cloud hosting) that is itself controlled by the same small ecosystem of tech companies, and sustain itself without the advertising revenue that flows to platforms with the largest user bases. This is not a realistic option. It is a thought-terminating cliché.

Second, we already reject the "private company" argument in dozens of other contexts. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 told private businesses that they could not refuse service on the basis of race. Common carrier doctrine has for centuries required privately operated transportation and communication networks to serve all comers without discrimination. The Americans with Disabilities Act requires private businesses to make accommodations for disabled customers. We do not allow restaurants to refuse to serve Black patrons and then tell those patrons to "build your own restaurant." We recognize that when private entities operate at a certain scale and serve a certain public function, the public interest constrains their discretion.

Third, the platforms themselves have invited this treatment. They lobbied for and received Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which shields them from liability for user-generated content on the theory that they are not publishers making editorial judgments—they are neutral conduits for speech. But you cannot simultaneously claim to be a neutral platform (entitled to legal immunity) and claim to be a publisher making editorial choices (entitled to editorial discretion). If platforms want the legal protections of a common carrier, they must accept the obligations of one.

IV. Moderation Cannot Solve the Problems It Claims to Address

Defenders of content moderation argue that without it, platforms would be overrun by spam, harassment, fraud, and dangerous misinformation. Let us examine each of these claims.

Spam and fraud are already illegal. Fraud, identity theft, and scam operations violate existing criminal and civil law. Platforms can and should cooperate with law enforcement to address illegal activity, just as telephone companies cooperate with law enforcement to address illegal activity conducted over phone lines—without listening to every call and deciding which conversations are permitted.

Harassment and threats are already illegal in virtually every jurisdiction. Stalking, credible threats of violence, doxxing, and targeted campaigns of abuse violate existing law. Requiring platforms to host lawful speech does not mean requiring them to host illegal speech. The distinction is clear, well-established, and adjudicated by courts—not by corporate trust-and-safety teams.

"Misinformation" is the most dangerous justification for content moderation, because it is the most subjective. Who decides what constitutes misinformation? During the COVID-19 pandemic, platforms removed posts suggesting that the virus may have originated in a Chinese laboratory—a theory that was initially dismissed as conspiracy but has since gained serious credibility and is now investigated by multiple governments. Platforms removed posts questioning the efficacy of cloth masks—a position subsequently supported by rigorous studies. Platforms removed posts expressing skepticism about the durability of natural immunity—a position subsequently validated by scientific consensus. In each case, the "misinformation" label was applied to speech that turned out to be at least partially correct, or at least reasonable to discuss.

The history of science is a history of dissenting views that were initially ridiculed and later vindicated. A regime in which corporate boards and algorithmic classifiers decide which scientific hypotheses may and may not be discussed is a regime that is hostile to science itself. The answer to bad information is more information, not censorship. Sunlight is the best disinfectant; forced silence breeds only suspicion and conspiracy.

V. Selective Enforcement Is the Norm, Not the Exception

Even if one believed that content moderation could theoretically be applied neutrally, the empirical reality is that it is applied selectively and politically. Platforms consistently enforce their rules more aggressively against disfavored political viewpoints and more leniently against favored ones. This is not a partisan claim—it is a complaint heard across the political spectrum.

Conservatives have documented cases where their content is removed or suppressed while equivalent content from progressive voices remains. Progressives have documented cases where far-right extremism flourishes on platforms while left-wing organizing is suppressed. International users have documented cases where speech critical of the ruling government of a lucrative market (such as India or China) is moderated at the behest of that government, while speech critical of less commercially important regimes is allowed to stand.

This selective enforcement is not an aberration that can be fixed by better policies. It is the inevitable consequence of granting any entity the discretionary power to decide what speech is acceptable. Power, once granted, will be exercised in the interest of the powerful. The only way to prevent selective enforcement is to eliminate the discretion that makes it possible.

VI. The Global Stakes Are Enormous

The United States is not the only country affected by platform moderation decisions. For billions of people in authoritarian and semi-authoritarian regimes, social media platforms are the only space where they can speak freely. And yet platforms routinely comply with government takedown requests from authoritarian regimes, removing dissident speech, protest organizing, and criticism of ruling parties.

If platforms were legally required to host all lawful speech—and if "lawful" were defined robustly to include speech protected by international human rights norms—the effect would be transformative. Platforms would be forced to become genuine havens of free expression worldwide, rather than tools of censorship that bend to the will of whatever government applies the most pressure.

Moreover, the current moderation regime gives authoritarian governments a template for internet censorship. When democracies demonstrate that speech can and should be regulated by powerful gatekeepers, they provide a model that authoritarian states eagerly adopt and expand. The global free speech community has watched in horror as the European Union's Digital Services Act, India's IT Rules, and similar regulatory frameworks in other democracies have been cited as justifications for censorship by governments in Turkey, Russia, and beyond. The answer is not to expand moderation but to establish an inviolable principle: platforms must carry all lawful speech, everywhere.

VII. The Marketplace of Ideas Works

The deepest argument against content moderation is also the simplest: the marketplace of ideas works. It has always worked. It is messy, uncomfortable, and sometimes painful. It means encountering views you find repugnant, hearing arguments you believe are wrong, and confronting perspectives that challenge your own. But it is precisely this friction that produces knowledge, progress, and democratic accountability.

John Stuart Mill argued in On Liberty that even false ideas serve a vital purpose: by engaging with them, we sharpen and deepen our understanding of the truth. Even the most offensive and outrageous speech serves a function: it reveals the state of public opinion, allows us to identify and confront dangerous ideas openly rather than driving them underground, and tests our commitment to our own principles.

History confirms Mill's reasoning. Every major advance in human thought—from the abolition of slavery to women's suffrage to civil rights to marriage equality—was once considered dangerous, offensive, or "harmful" by the mainstream of opinion. Every one of these advances required people to express views that the powerful found threatening. A regime of content moderation, had it existed at the time, would have suppressed every one of them.

The cure for bad speech is not silence. The cure for bad speech is more speech. This principle has served free societies well for centuries. There is no reason to abandon it now, and every reason to extend it to the digital spaces where our public discourse increasingly takes place.

VIII. A Proposed Framework

To be concrete, I propose the following:

  1. Any platform exceeding a threshold of users or public reach (e.g., 50 million monthly active users) should be legally classified as a common carrier or public forum.

  2. Such platforms must carry all speech that is lawful under the jurisdiction in which the user is located. Speech that violates existing criminal law (credible threats of violence, fraud, child sexual abuse material) is not protected and can be removed in cooperation with law enforcement.

  3. Platforms retain the right to curate presentation—algorithmic ranking, recommendation systems, and user-controlled filtering tools can and should exist. Users should be empowered to choose what they see. But removal of lawful speech should be prohibited.

  4. Platforms must provide transparent, auditable processes for any content that is removed as illegal, with independent oversight and meaningful appeals.

  5. Section 230 protections should be conditioned on compliance with these obligations. Platforms that wish to act as publishers and make editorial judgments may do so—but they must accept the corresponding liability.

This framework preserves the legitimate functions of moderation (removing genuinely illegal content, empowering user choice) while eliminating the illegitimate ones (discretionary suppression of lawful speech based on corporate preference).

Conclusion: The Courage to Be Uncomfortable

The impulse to moderate content is understandable. The internet is a big, loud, chaotic place, and much of what appears on it is ugly, wrong, or offensive. The desire to clean it up—to create a sanitized, pleasant, "safe" online environment—is natural and well-intentioned.

But good intentions are not enough. The road to censorship is always paved with good intentions. Every authoritarian regime in history has justified its suppression of speech by appealing to the need for social harmony, public safety, or the prevention of harm. The question is never whether those in power believe censorship is justified—they always do. The question is whether we trust any entity, public or private, with the power to decide what the rest of us may think and say.

We should not. Not our government, and not a handful of unaccountable corporations in Silicon Valley. The answer to the challenges of the digital age is not more control over speech but less. It is to trust the public—messy, contradictory, often wrongheaded as we are—with the freedom to speak, to listen, to argue, to persuade, and to be persuaded. It is to have the courage to be uncomfortable, because the alternative—a world in which our most important conversations are filtered through the preferences of corporate censors—is far more dangerous than anything any troll, crank, or extremist could ever post.

Free speech is not a problem to be managed. It is the foundation upon which every other freedom rests. It is time we extended that foundation to the digital world—not as a courtesy granted by benevolent platforms, but as a right guaranteed by law.

Readers are encouraged to consider counterarguments, including concerns about harassment, radicalization, child safety, and the practical challenges of implementing such a framework, before forming their own views.

Arguments for Social Media as Neutral Common Carriers

This is a genuinely debated policy position with several interconnected strands of reasoning. Here's a thorough presentation of the case proponents make:

1. The "Modern Public Square" Argument

Proponents argue that social media platforms have effectively become the dominant venues for public discourse — analogous to town squares, parks, or other traditional public forums. A small number of companies (Meta, X/Twitter, YouTube, TikTok) control the infrastructure through which billions of people communicate, organize politically, access news, and participate in civic life.

The argument holds that when private entities achieve this level of dominance over public discourse, the functional effect of their censorship decisions becomes indistinguishable from government censorship in its impact — even if it doesn't trigger First Amendment protections legally. People silenced on major platforms may lose access to audiences, economic opportunities, and political influence in ways that are effectively coercive.

2. The Common Carrier / Public Utility Analogy

Historically, certain private businesses that serve essential public functions — railroads, telegraph companies, telephone companies, ISPs — have been classified as common carriers legally obligated to serve all customers without discrimination. The rationale is that when a business becomes so essential to public life that people effectively cannot avoid it, allowing it to refuse service based on its own preferences creates dangerous concentrations of private power.

Proponents argue social media platforms meet this threshold because of network effects: a platform's value comes from the fact that everyone else is already there. "Just build your own platform" is dismissed as impractical — Parler, Gab, and others have illustrated how difficult it is to compete when the dominant platforms control not just users but also app stores, cloud hosting, payment processors, and advertiser networks.

The analogy to phone companies is particularly central: we don't allow AT&T to cut off your phone service because it dislikes what you said in a phone call, even if what you said was offensive or misleading. Proponents argue the same logic should apply to social media.

3. Viewpoint Discrimination Concerns

A core concern is that content moderation, however it's described in policy documents, inevitably involves viewpoint discrimination in practice. Proponents point to several patterns:

  • Inconsistent enforcement: Rules against "misinformation" or "hate speech" are applied more aggressively against some ideological perspectives than others, suggesting the rules serve as pretexts for viewpoint-based suppression.
  • Vague standards: Terms like "harmful," "misleading," or "community standards" are sufficiently ambiguous that they give platforms essentially unlimited discretion to remove content.
  • Opaque processes: Moderation decisions are often made by low-level reviewers applying inconsistent interpretations, with limited meaningful appeal processes.
  • Chilling effects: Even when enforcement is sporadic, the threat of removal or deplatforming causes widespread self-censorship, which may be more damaging than the actual removals.

The argument is that no private entity should wield this kind of discretionary power over public discourse, regardless of whether that power is exercised through explicit ideology or implicit bias.

4. Section 230 and the "Deal" Argument

Some proponents frame this as a matter of logical consistency with existing law. Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act gives platforms immunity from liability for user-generated content — treating them as distributors rather than publishers. The argument is that this immunity was granted precisely because platforms were understood to be neutral conduits, not editorial voices.

If platforms instead act as editors — making sophisticated, judgment-based decisions about which viewpoints to amplify and which to suppress — proponents argue they should be treated as publishers and lose their immunity. The current arrangement is characterized as the "worst of both worlds": platforms exercise editorial discretion without bearing any corresponding editorial liability.

5. Democratic and Anti-Authoritarian Concerns

Proponents argue that concentrating control over public discourse in the hands of a few unaccountable Silicon Valley executives is inherently dangerous to democracy, regardless of which party those executives currently favor. Key concerns include:

  • Accountability gap: Platform CEOs and trust-and-safety teams aren't elected, can't be voted out, and face no constitutional constraints. Their decisions affect democratic participation more directly than many government actions, yet citizens have no formal recourse.
  • Precedent risk: Whatever political faction benefits from current moderation practices, the power to censor could be redirected at any time. Those who cheer censorship of their opponents today may find themselves silenced tomorrow.
  • Global implications: US-based platforms exercise enormous influence over political discourse worldwide, often imposing American cultural norms on societies with very different traditions and values.

6. Practical and Epistemological Arguments Against Moderation

Some proponents make pragmatic claims:

  • Truth is best determined through open discourse, not gatekeeping. Suppressing "misinformation" assumes infallible knowledge of what's true — a dangerous assumption, as demonstrated when platforms suppressed content (e.g., the Wuhan lab leak hypothesis, certain COVID policy debates) that later proved legitimate.
  • Counter-speech is more effective than censorship in changing minds and correcting errors.
  • Moderation at scale is inherently impossible to do well — automated systems make absurd errors, human reviewers are overworked and inconsistent, and the sheer volume of content guarantees both over- and under-enforcement.

7. Economic and Competition Arguments

Some proponents argue that neutral platform obligations would actually improve market competition by removing platforms' ability to use content policies as competitive weapons — for instance, suppressing links to competing services or favoring partners' content.

Important Context

It's worth noting that this position has significant counterarguments that proponents don't always engage with:

  • Platforms have legitimate interests in removing spam, fraud, harassment, CSAM, and coordinated inauthentic behavior that a pure neutrality mandate would complicate.
  • "Legal content" includes a vast amount of material most users don't want to see.
  • The common carrier analogy is imperfect — phone calls are private; social media posts are published to mass audiences.
  • Truly unmoderated platforms (like early 8chan) have tended to attract extreme content that drives away mainstream users, potentially undermining the very public-square function proponents value.
  • There are genuine free-speech interests on both sides — forced hosting of certain content may compel platforms to associate with speech they find objectionable, raising their own expressive freedom concerns.

This remains one of the most actively contested questions in technology policy, internet law, and political philosophy, with thoughtful people on multiple sides.

The Case for Abolishing Content Moderation: Why Tech Platforms Must Host All Lawful Speech

Introduction

In the span of two decades, a handful of private corporations have assumed a role once reserved for governments and public squares: gatekeepers of human discourse. Meta, Google, X, TikTok, and a few others now determine what billions of people can say, see, and share. When these companies moderate content beyond what the law requires, they exercise a form of power that is unaccountable, inconsistent, and fundamentally incompatible with a free society. The time has come to legally require digital platforms to host all lawful speech, abolishing the discretionary content moderation regimes that have transformed our digital public square into a patchwork of corporate fiefdoms. Absolute protection for lawful expression online is not a radical proposition—it is the logical extension of the free-speech principles that have underwritten democratic life for centuries.

The Public Square Has Moved, and the Law Must Follow

The First Amendment protects Americans from government censorship, but it was drafted in an age when the public square was a physical place—a town green, a printing press, a soapbox. Today, political organizing, journalism, scientific debate, religious expression, and ordinary conversation occur overwhelmingly on privately owned platforms. When Facebook, YouTube, or X removes a user or a post, the practical effect on that speaker's ability to reach an audience is often greater than any government restriction could impose.

Justice Clarence Thomas, in his concurrence in Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute (2021), observed that the dominant digital platforms bear striking resemblance to common carriers and traditional places of public accommodation. Common carriers—telephone companies, railroads, postal services—have long been required by law to serve all customers without discrimination. They cannot refuse to carry a phone call because they dislike the opinions being expressed. Major social media platforms, which have achieved scale, network effects, and market power comparable to these utilities, should be subject to the same nondiscrimination requirements. If the telephone company cannot cut your line for expressing unpopular political views, neither should Twitter be able to delete your account for the same reason.

Content Moderation Has Proven Biased, Arbitrary, and Unaccountable

Defenders of the status quo often claim that platforms apply neutral, transparent rules. The evidence suggests otherwise. Internal documents revealed through lawsuits and whistleblowers—the Twitter Files, the Facebook Files, and disclosures from former trust-and-safety employees—have repeatedly shown that moderation decisions are influenced by political pressure, ideological bias among staff, and opaque "shadow banning" practices users cannot even detect, let alone appeal.

Consider the now-infamous suppression of the Hunter Biden laptop story in October 2020, which Twitter and Facebook throttled on the basis of a "hack and leak" theory that was never substantiated. Consider the removal of posts questioning the natural-origin hypothesis of COVID-19—a position once labeled "misinformation" and now considered a legitimate scientific hypothesis taken seriously by the U.S. Department of Energy and FBI. Consider the suspension of doctors, scientists, and journalists whose heterodox views were later vindicated. In each case, platforms arrogated to themselves the power to declare truth, and in each case, they failed.

The problem is not that moderators are uniquely malicious. It is that the task they have assumed is impossible. No group of trust-and-safety officials in San Francisco can reliably distinguish truth from falsehood in real time across every contested domain of human inquiry. Their attempts to do so inevitably reflect the biases of their institution, their class, and their political milieu. Free expression is not valuable despite our epistemic uncertainty—it is valuable because of it. When we do not know with certainty what is true, we must allow all claims to compete in open debate.

Counter-Speech, Not Censorship, Is the Answer to Bad Speech

The classical liberal answer to harmful or false speech has always been more speech, not enforced silence. Louis Brandeis articulated this principle in Whitney v. California: "If there be time to expose through discussion the falsehood and fallacies, to avert the evil by the processes of education, the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence."

On a platform governed by a hosting mandate, counter-speech does not disappear—it flourishes. Falsehoods can be rebutted, conspiracy theories can be debunked, and bigotry can be confronted by those who disagree. Indeed, research on "inoculation" against misinformation suggests that exposure to bad arguments alongside good ones builds greater epistemic resilience than censorship, which often confers forbidden-knowledge allure on the censored material and erodes trust in institutions that engage in it. The most reliable long-term defense against bad ideas is a citizenry accustomed to wrestling with them.

Moreover, users retain abundant tools to curate their own experience: blocking, muting, filtering by keyword, following and unfollowing, and using third-party moderation layers. A hosting mandate does not force any user to read any particular content. It merely prevents the platform itself from making that decision unilaterally for everyone.

Selective Enforcement Corrupts Discourse

Even if one believes some moderation is desirable in principle, the selective application of moderation rules is corrosive in practice. When platforms enforce rules against some users and not others—protecting the speech of favored constituencies while punishing disfavored ones—they do not merely fail at neutrality. They actively tilt the playing field of public debate. Voters form opinions, politicians win elections, and social movements succeed or fail based on what trends, what gets amplified, and what gets suppressed. Discretionary moderation makes these outcomes partly a function of corporate preference rather than democratic deliberation.

A legal requirement to host all lawful speech eliminates this problem at the root. There would be no ambiguous "hate speech" rules to apply inconsistently, no "misinformation" judgments that shift with political winds, no special carve-outs for politicians or celebrities. The rule would be simple: if speech is legal, platforms must host it.

Addressing the Objections

Won't platforms become unusable cesspools? Spam, harassment targeting specific individuals, and genuine threats are all already illegal or subject to narrow, clearly defined restrictions.
